analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from using credit checks to deny people jobs or promotions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee for the rest of the 111th Congress, with one subcommittee hearing and no markup or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to stop employers from pulling credit reports on job applicants or current employees for hiring, firing, or other adverse decisions. It would ban the practice even when the worker consents, with narrow exceptions for jobs requiring national security or FDIC clearance, some government positions, and financial-institution executives. People with medical debt, job loss, or divorce on their credit file would no longer face a second penalty when applying for work.
analysis.who_benefits: Job applicants and current workers whose credit histories include unemployment, medical debt, divorce, or other hardships would no longer be screened out of jobs because of their credit score. Consumer and civil rights groups argue credit checks fall hardest on low-income workers and disproportionately harm Black and Hispanic applicants, who are likelier to have damaged credit through no fault of character.

how_it_helps.text: It bars employers from using or even requesting a credit report for employment decisions, even with the applicant's consent.
It amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that any report containing information on creditworthiness cannot be used for hiring, firing, or adverse action, except for a narrow set of jobs.
Job seekers recovering from unemployment, medical debt, or divorce would no longer face a catch-22 in which bad credit — often caused by job loss — blocks them from getting a job.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would lose a screening tool they currently use, and credit reporting agencies and background-check firms would lose a slice of revenue from selling employment credit reports.

drawbacks.text: Even supporters acknowledge some jobs warrant a look at an applicant's finances; the bill's own exceptions for national security, FDIC clearance, government agencies, and financial executives show a limit on how broadly a blanket ban can safely extend.
Employers argue credit history can reveal signs of theft or financial irresponsibility relevant to positions of trust; the bill would bar that screen even with an applicant's consent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits for job seekers with damaged credit are real but targeted; the drawbacks are modest: employers lose one screening tool, and some argue a credit history can flag fiduciary risk, which the exceptions partially cover. It died without amendment or a vote, so its actual impact was zero and the costs were never tested in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2009, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and was never brought to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 9, 2009 and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The only action after that was a subcommittee hearing on financial institutions and consumer credit in September 2010 — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The bill died in committee at the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies and background-screening firms that sell employment credit checks keep that business, and employers keep a cheap screening tool; job seekers with bad credit remain exposed to it.

for.name: Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the Financial Services Committee.

for.name: Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
for.what_they_did: Held one hearing on the bill in September 2010, its only action.

sides.party_line_note: All 56 cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: Employment screening is a steady revenue stream for credit bureaus; banning employer credit checks would shrink that market. Their interest runs against job applicants who pay the price of the screening.

industries.industry: Background screening and HR services firms
industries.note: Firms that sell employment credit reports would lose a product line if employers can no longer pull credit files on candidates.

industries.industry: Employers (retail, staffing, and other large private-sector employers)
industries.note: Employers would lose access to a cheap screening tool, though for most the loss is convenience rather than core operations.
